extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, political scientists, and policymakers interested in public opinion and the role of the press
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length theoretical treatment of how public opinions are formed, the limits on public access to facts, and how news/propaganda and institutional arrangements shape the 'pseudo-environment' that guides behavior. Useful for evaluating news practices, propaganda, and the institutional requirements for informed democratic decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship and privacy as information barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Without some form of censorship, propaganda in the strict sense of the word is impossible. Privacy and official secrecy create barriers between the public and events; what is concealed may be treated as 'none of the public's business.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes military censorship, legal privileges (doctor–patient, lawyer–client), government control of cables/passports/mails, and the elastic social notion of privacy (e.g., salaries vs. wages, corporate profits). Example: wartime military censorship at Verdun. Use this criterion to evaluate whether independent access to facts was limited and how that limitation could enable manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of selection and framing by authorities (propaganda)
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of men who can prevent independent access to the event arrange the news of it to suit their purpose; they select facts and frame narratives to produce desired inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by French General Staff communiques at Verdun: omission of inconvenient facts, choice of adjectives/phrasing to steady public morale, and deliberate use of certain narratives (e.g., attrition thesis). Guidance includes looking for evidence of selective omission, editorial intervention by authorities, and deliberate framing choices that steer conclusions without explicit argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-environment: internal pictures determine action
rubrics_metrics.description: What each man does is based not on direct and certain knowledge, but on pictures made by himself or given to him. 'The way in which the world is imagined determines at any particular moment what men will do.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: maps that mislead explorers, propaganda that creates class consciousness or national sentiment. Use this criterion to assess how representations (mental images, stereotyped narratives) — rather than objective facts — shape behavior, effort, hopes and immediate responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact and opportunity: limits on circulation of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: There are distinct limits upon the circulation of ideas — whole sections and enclaves hear only vaguely about much that is going on; reaching 'everybody' requires massive organized effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical examples (Creel Committee machinery, Four Minute Men, posters, organizational distribution). Consider transport and communications infrastructure (railroads, cables, ports), economic costs, and institutional channels; evaluate reach and distribution mechanisms when judging how representative a reported 'public opinion' really is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and attention: compression and distortion of events
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparatively meager time available in each day for paying attention to public affairs and the need to compress events into very short messages distort information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short messages, headlines and limited attention force simplification; small vocabularies must express complicated worlds, creating distortions. Use this to evaluate whether necessary complexity has been lost in condensed reports and whether simplification yields misleading impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed, words, and clearness (message mechanics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events must be explored, reported, and imagined; press and official messages use specific words and speeds of transmission that shape how the public conceives situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine choice of wording (nouns/adjectives/verbs), tempo of release, and placement. Example: editorial conferences where generals debated phrasing of communiques; choice to include or exclude von Deimling's order. Assess how linguistic choices aid or bias comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and quantitative presentation as persuasive technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant repetition of formulas and casualty statistics produces striking effects and impressions that shape belief (e.g., Major Cointet's increasing German-loss figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for repeated statistics, recurring formulaic phrases, and calculated numerical presentations designed to create an impression rather than to present balanced evidence. Repetition can magnify an inference even when evidentiary basis is weak or selective; evaluate provenance and method of such figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infrastructure and monopolies as structural barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopolizing cables, ports, fuel stations, passes, canals, terminals and the like creates barriers upon exchange of news and opinion; cost and limited supply also restrict circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how ownership and control of physical and communication infrastructure (and related economic policies like tariffs/subsidies) affect who gets information and who is excluded. This is a criterion for systemic evaluation of information access, not just a momentary editorial choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for independent expert organization to represent unseen facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative government cannot be worked successfully unless there is an independent, expert organization for making the unseen facts intelligible to those who must make decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that press and mass readership cannot substitute for expert representation of complex unseen facts. Use this to evaluate institutional arrangements: whether decisions are supported by independent expert analysis, and whether the press is being unfairly relied upon to provide what only expert inquiry can supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source provenance questioning (critical source scrutiny)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is illuminating to ask how you got at the facts on which you base your opinion: who actually saw, heard, counted, named the thing; how much was he permitted to see; where was he when he watched it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical diagnostic: trace the chain of reporting, ask about access and vantage point, interrogate the sampling of people or places reported on. Use this criterion to judge credibility and representativeness of reported facts and to guard against unexamined distance between opinion and event.
